name: AI / ML Engineer
tagline: Build, evaluate and ship machine-learning systems and LLM applications.
description: For anyone who wants to build machine-learning products, from classic models to LLM-powered applications and agents, and run them reliably in production. You begin with the maths and programming, work through core ML, deep learning, NLP and transformers, then prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, evaluation and agents, and finish with MLOps, inference and responsible AI.
outcomes: Frame a business problem as an ML task, build a baseline and evaluate it honestly with the right metrics and validation
Implement and train neural networks, including CNNs and transformers, in a modern deep-learning framework
Build LLM applications with prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, tool-using agents and systematic evaluation
Fine-tune a pretrained model for a task and judge whether that beats prompting or RAG
Package, deploy, optimise and monitor models in production with an MLOps pipeline
Assess a system for fairness, robustness, privacy and safety risks and explain its predictions

stages.name: Mathematical foundations
stages.description: Algebra to calculus and linear algebra, the language every model is written in.

items.why: Fractions, exponents and logarithm-ready number sense for everything that follows.
Functions and equations; a model is a function with tunable parameters.
Just the geometry that trigonometry and vectors build on.
Angles and the unit circle for cosine similarity and positional encodings.
Exponentials and logs are everywhere in ML: softmax, log-likelihood, learning-rate schedules.
Vectors, lines and planes: a linear classifier is a hyperplane.
Derivatives and the chain rule are how models learn.
Gradients, Jacobians and partial derivatives drive gradient descent in millions of dimensions.
Data are matrices, layers are matrix multiplies and embeddings are vectors; this is the core ML maths.

stages.name: Probability, statistics & optimisation
stages.description: Reason about uncertainty, evaluate models properly and understand how training optimises them.

items.why: Summarising data with distributions, averages and spread comes before modelling.
Events, conditional probability and Bayes' rule, the starting point for probabilistic models.
Random variables, expectations and distributions underpin loss functions and generative models.
Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests tell you whether a model improvement is real.
Linear and logistic regression are the first ML models and the baseline you should always try.
Priors, posteriors and approximate inference for principled uncertainty.
Optimality conditions, convexity and Lagrange multipliers behind training objectives.
SGD, momentum, Adam and backpropagation: how networks are actually trained.
Risk, generalisation, bias-variance and model selection: the theory of why ML works.

stages.name: Programming & data tooling
stages.description: Python, data structures and the data stack you'll use every day.

items.why: How computers represent and process data, before writing code.
Python is the language of ML; fluency here pays off in every later stage.
Environments, GPUs and remote training jobs are managed from the shell.
Code, experiments and collaboration all run through Git.
Structuring code into clean functions and modules instead of one giant notebook.
PyTorch modules, datasets and most ML libraries are class-based.
Logic, counting, graphs and asymptotic notation for data structures and algorithms.
Hash maps, heaps, trees and graphs appear in tokenisers, retrieval indexes and data pipelines.
Algorithmic cost matters when data has billions of rows or a vector index millions of entries.
NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, notebooks and plotting, the daily ML toolkit.
SQL for getting training data, and vector databases for retrieval.
A practitioner's recap tying the maths to code: SVD, the chain rule and hypothesis tests in practice.
Looking hard at the data before modelling catches most problems early.

stages.name: Core machine learning
stages.description: Supervised and unsupervised learning, features and honest evaluation.

items.why: The big picture of what ML can and can't do, before the details.
Agents, paradigms and the history that explains how AI got where it is today.
Training, validation, loss, overfitting and generalisation in practice.
Cleaning, encoding, scaling and building features often matters more than the model.
Regression, classification, clustering and dimensionality reduction: the algorithm toolbox.
Metrics, cross-validation, leakage and statistical comparison keep you honest.
Gradient-boosted trees still win on tabular data, which covers most business problems.
Bayesian reasoning and graphical models for handling uncertainty.
Latent-variable models, EM and variational inference, the basis of VAEs and diffusion.

stages.name: Deep learning & computer vision
stages.description: Neural networks from first principles to CNNs, transformers and generative models.

items.why: Perceptrons, backpropagation, activations and losses: how a network learns.
PyTorch (and friends): tensors, autograd, data loaders and training loops.
Why training converges or doesn't: non-convex, stochastic and second-order methods.
Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence are the loss functions of modern ML.
Dropout, weight decay, batch and layer norm make deep networks trainable.
Convolutions and residual networks, the backbone of vision models.
Pixels, colour spaces, filtering and augmentation, needed for any vision pipeline.
Classification, detection and segmentation: the everyday computer-vision tasks.
Sequence modelling with RNNs and LSTMs, the problem transformers were built to solve.
Self-attention and the transformer, the architecture behind LLMs and modern vision.
Contrastive and masked pretraining produce the embeddings behind search and RAG.
VAEs, GANs and diffusion models for generating images, audio and data.

stages.name: NLP & large language models
stages.description: From text processing to how LLMs are pretrained and aligned.

items.why: Tokenisation and text normalisation, including the subword tokenisers LLMs use.
TF-IDF, n-grams and classic classifiers: strong baselines and the basis of keyword search in hybrid RAG.
Word and sentence embeddings are the foundation of semantic search.
Classification, NER, summarisation, QA and translation, the tasks LLMs are applied to.
MDPs, rewards and policies, the background you need for RLHF and for agents.
Pretraining, scaling laws, instruction tuning and RLHF: how LLMs are made and why they behave as they do.
Combining text, images and audio in one model.
Models that read images and documents, now standard in LLM applications.

stages.name: Building LLM applications
stages.description: Prompting, retrieval, agents, evaluation and fine-tuning: the LLM engineer's core toolkit.

items.why: Few-shot, chain-of-thought, structured output and injection defences for dependable prompts.
LLM APIs, tool calling, streaming, caching and cost and latency trade-offs in real products.
Chunking, embeddings, vector search, reranking and grounding answers in your own data.
Tool-using agents, planning loops, memory and multi-agent orchestration.
Eval sets, LLM-as-judge, benchmarks and regression testing, which make LLM work engineering and not guesswork.
SFT, LoRA, preference tuning and distillation for when prompting and RAG aren't enough.

stages.name: MLOps, systems & deployment
stages.description: Take models from notebook to reliable, efficient production systems.

items.why: Production ML code needs modular design, code review and good debugging habits.
Unit and integration tests for data pipelines, features and model services.
Number formats and memory hierarchy explain FP16/INT8 and why models are memory-bound.
Memory, processes and linking, enough to debug native ML libraries and CUDA builds.
Caches, SIMD, GPUs and memory bandwidth decide training and inference speed.
Processes, threads, memory and I/O on the machines that serve your models.
Docker images are how models are packaged and deployed.
Experiment tracking, data and model versioning, registries and pipelines.
Serving models behind APIs, batch versus online inference, and Kubernetes.
Shipping an LLM feature is the start; tracing, guardrails and cost control keep it alive in production.
Detecting drift, degraded quality and failures once a model is live.
Pipelines, warehouses and feature stores that feed training and inference.
GPUs, TPUs, CUDA and the roofline model, the hardware your budget buys.
Quantisation, distillation, batching and vLLM-style serving make models fast and affordable.
Managed ML services on AWS, GCP and Azure for training and serving at scale.

stages.name: Responsible AI
stages.description: Build systems that are fair, explainable, robust, private and safe.

items.why: Regulation such as the EU AI Act, and the governance processes organisations now require.
Measuring and mitigating bias across groups affected by your model.
SHAP, attribution and mechanistic methods for explaining predictions.
Adversarial examples, data poisoning and attacks on ML systems, including LLMs.
Differential privacy, federated learning and protecting training data.
Alignment, reward hacking and the safety of increasingly capable systems.

stages.name: Electives
stages.description: Specialisations that build on the core: reinforcement learning, recommenders, time series and more.

items.why: Elective (RL): policy and value iteration, the exact solutions to MDPs.
Elective (RL): learning values from sampled episodes.
Elective (RL): TD learning, Q-learning and policy gradients.
Elective (RL): DQN, PPO and actor-critic methods, also used in RLHF.
Elective: collaborative filtering, two-tower retrieval and ranking for feeds and stores.
Elective (time series): autocorrelation, stationarity and ARIMA.
Elective (time series): ML and deep-learning forecasting for demand, finance and sensors.
Elective: fraud, fault and intrusion detection with little labelled data.
Elective: estimating the effects of interventions, beyond correlation.
